RagShortTexts: In 1260 at Ain Jalut, Mamluk horse archers crushed Kitbuqa, definitively halting Mongol.

Variants.Content: Mongol armies had overrun Persia, Armenia, and much of Syria before 1260, and their horsemen seemed impossible to stop. On September 3, 1260, Mamluk Sultan Qutuz and his commander Baibars met the Ilkhanate general Kitbuqa at Ain Jalut, a spring in the Galilee plain. The Mamluks feigned a retreat to draw the Mongol vanguard into the open, then turned on it in a close cavalry counter-attack while archers and massed horsemen wore the enemy down. Kitbuqa was captured and later executed. The battle halted the Mongol advance toward Egypt and showed that disciplined mounted archers could beat the Mongol army in the field, a lesson that shaped Mamluk tactics for decades.

Ain Jalut saved Cairo and Damascus from Mongol conquest and gave the Mamluk regime the prestige to rule Egypt and Syria. For an emir, the victory meant new iqta grants and a fresh claim to command. Soldiers remember the Galilee dust, the thirst, and the final charge that broke the Mongol line.
